items.title: Phil Woods interviewed by Monk Rowe, Delaware Water Gap, PA, November 8, 1999
items.q: I think it’s going to be more — a typical set might be a tango, an Astor Piazzolla, a bossa nova... I could conceivably play that dream set I was talking about playing, a Piazzolla

ctx.x: Do you feel jazz is healthier today than it has been in the past?

No, not really healthier. I think it’s become — I don’t mean to paint a bleak picture — but jazz seems to have lost its cutting edge, it seems to be in a regressive mode activated © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

somehow. I mean jazz just goes on, and it’s never been so alive and well, we’ve never had so many kids playing music, and this is a positive thing. I don’t mean to negate the import of a kid picking up an instrument because if he’s got an instrument in his mouth he’s probably less liable to buy an assault rifle. I mean I think music is good. Any cutting back of funds for music education is a big mistake, which we’re also getting involved in. But the idea of jazz being alive and well, every campus has a jazz…

items.title: Phil Woods — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: the children of Astor Piazzola, who was the Charlie Parker of the tango.

ctx.x: Mmm hmmm. You mentioned Charles Ives. It makes me think … jazz musicians should listen to other jazz musicians but what else should a jazz musician do if they really want to …

Oh, read a book. [laughs] Go to a museum. Learn a language. Visit other cultures; understand how other societies work. Don’t be so myopic about your musical tastes. Listen to music that you don’t even like. If you don’t like something, listen to it and find out why you don’t like it. You might end up liking it, you know? Stretch your ears, don’t get in that comfort zone. uh A lot of jazz musicians are lazy, you know. They get into a bag and say I mean some musicians say, “Oh, I don’t want to read,” you know,…

to be able to read a little bit, you know. Learn some keyboard, learn some keyboard harmony. Be able to write a little tune, understand fugal techniques, understand the Bach, Beethoven, Brahms. I mean, if you’re going to play bebop, um I mean, I think Bach is to fugal technique what Bird is to articulated bebop. That’s the epitome. So you got to, and you can equate the two; Bach and Bird have a lot in common, I think, you know, rhythmically and the contrast and the way the stuff swings. Bach swings like crazy.…
